title: The Very Big World Problem
subtitle: A Helpful Guide to Classroom Geography
dedication: To all the students who try their very best, even when they are not entirely sure what is happening.
back_cover_blurb: Chester, Marisol, and Winston are the very best of friends! Join them as they learn a valuable lesson about geography, cooperation, and the importance of reading the fine print on a custom order.
moral: It is always better to have a map than to be lost, unless the map is large enough to flatten the mayor's podium.
premise_seed: The gang breaks a classroom globe and decides to replace it before anyone notices, instead of just saying sorry.

cast.name: Chester Antialiased
cast.micro_emotion: Nodding politely with wide frozen eyes after asking 'what?' twice and still not catching a word.
cast.visual_description: A lanky green-skinned pixel-art goblin-boy with an oversized blocky chin, one raised eyebrow, giant nervously wide square eyes, crooked metal braces, and messy spiky teal pixel hair, wearing a burgundy high school polo shirt with a crooked yellow lanyard
cast.superlative: Most Likely To Nod Along In Silence
cast.quote: Haha yeah totally (I did not hear a single syllable).

cast.name: Marisol Brittle
cast.micro_emotion: Wide-eyed determined exhaustion after alphabetizing her spice rack instead of studying for finals.
cast.visual_description: A slightly lopsided terracotta-and-lavender plasticine clay owl-humanoid figurine with visible fingerprint smudges, giant mismatched sculpted eyes with tiny dark bags underneath, and crooked wire spectacles, wearing a miniature hand-knit mustard varsity cardigan
cast.superlative: Most Likely To Start A Hobby At 2 AM
cast.quote: Sleep is temporary, color-coded Google Docs are forever.

cast.name: Winston Crumb
cast.micro_emotion: The thousand-yard stare of someone who just heard the microwave beep two seconds before they reached it.
cast.visual_description: A fuzzy chartreuse fleece puppet creature with a long cylindrical snout, oversized asymmetrical plastic googly eyes pointing slightly outward, wild tufts of orange yarn hair, and a tiny stitched 'o' mouth, wearing a crisp baby-blue Oxford shirt and navy sweater vest
cast.superlative: Most Likely To Jump At The Bell
cast.quote: I was promised this hallway would be quieter.

pages.text: Marisol and Winston saw the crack too. They decided to be seen cooperating, as it was the most socially acceptable way to spend a Tuesday. "We must replace it before the next bell rings!" said Marisol. They decided to work together, as it is the most efficient way to ensure no one person takes all the blame. They were very happy to be seen together.
pages.beat: The group is too terrified of the teacher's reaction to report it, so they decide to replace the globe before the next period.

logline: After accidentally breaking a classroom globe, three mismatched students attempt to replace it with an increasingly massive replica, leading to a city-wide cartographic crisis.
running_gag: Chester nodding politely while completely missing instructions, leading others to believe he has a master plan.
inciting_mistake: Chester accidentally knocks over the classroom globe while trying to see if it's 'anti-aliased', causing a small crack in the plastic.

writers_room.tone:
SECRET SUBTEXT: None of these three actually like each other very much, but they are far too oblivious to realize it. They genuinely believe they are best friends.

How to deliver it (all of it SLIGHT and SUBTLE, never stated outright, never mean-spirited):
- Backhanded compliments the speaker thinks are sincere ("You're so brave to wear that sweater vest, Winston.").
- Characters "helping" each other in ways that are really about themselves, and nobody notices.
- Tiny moments of polite avoidance: someone volunteers for the job that happens to be furthest from the others; someone gives a gift that is clearly re-gifted.
- They talk past each other and each walks away certain the conversation went great.
- The cheerful 1950s narrator is ever so faintly sarcastic, reporting their "friendship" with a deadpan straight face (e.g. "They were the very best of friends, which is to say they had all been assigned to the same table.").
- Sprinkle a few clever, quiet puns (on globes, the world, maps, spinning, axes, "falling out", etc.) that an adult catches and a child would miss. At most one pun per page, and never on consecutive pages. No groaners, no winking at the reader.
- The ending should reaffirm their "friendship" in a way that makes it clear (to the reader only) that they'd all happily never see each other again.

scores.why: Strongest escalation from a classroom mistake to urban planning and the most concrete visual payoff with the giant globe.
The auction plot is a detour that slows the momentum and feels disconnected from the school setting.
The zoning map idea is clever but the ventilation shaft sequence kills the visual scale of the 'Big World' theme.

notes_for_writers: Lean into the 'visual medium' clash: when Chester (pixel) tries to fix the smudge on the giant globe, have him try to 'delete' it by clicking his finger like a mouse or moving in 4-pixel increments for a specific comedic beat.

Sharpen the 'friendship' subtext: on Page 11, when sneaking the globe in, have them 'help' each other by pushing the other person toward the danger first, framed as 'giving them the honor of leading'.

Escalate the urban planning on Page 15: instead of just a committee, have Marisol actually redraw the town's street layout to be 'more efficient,' causing citizens to drive their cars into fountains because the globe's scale was off.
Add a subtle map pun on Page 17 during the parade, such as the narrator noting that the trio's friendship was 'reaching its axis,' or describing their coordination as 'completely off-center'.

The climax on Page 18 needs more visual chaos: the giant globe shouldn't just collapse, it should roll through the town square like a boulder from Indiana Jones, flattening specific civic landmarks (the 'World's Largest Yarn Ball', etc.) before hitting the podium.

Chester's internal monologue about the oven is a bit generic. Make it more 'pixel-brained'. Fix: 'Chester nodded politely, wondering if he could actually taste the color teal.'
The transition from 'leading the way' to being used as a 'human wedge' is abrupt. Add a line where Marisol compliments Winston's 'sturdy, felt-like density' before pushing him.
Winston finding the alarm 'refreshing' contradicts his character archetype of being alarmed by noise. Fix: He should trigger the alarm in a panic to drown out the engine, then immediately regret it.
The jump to 'city-wide committee' is a massive leap in stakes that isn't earned. Scale it back to the school board or a neighborhood association to keep the comedy grounded.

Logic hole: Chester cannot 'click' a physical object to resize it. Fix: Have him lean in too close (callback to Page 1) and accidentally trigger a release lever or push a precarious support beam with his blocky chin.

The globe 'crashing directly into the classroom' from the town square is a physical impossibility. Fix: The globe should roll down the main street, through the school gates, and smash into the classroom wall, creating a 'new window' that reveals the original globe.
The resolution is a bit soft. Add a subtle map pun to the moral or final line. Example: 'They were perfectly aligned, much like two tectonic plates just before a catastrophic shift.'

character-editor.biggest_problem: The characters are acting as a cohesive team rather than three socially incompatible strangers who happen to be in the same room. The 'secret subtext' of mutual dislike is missing; they are currently too helpful and cooperative.
keep: The 1950s narrator's earnest, deadpan voice
Chester's '16-bit' physical comedy (the chin impact)
The escalating absurdity of the globe size
Winston's sensory overload as a character driver

page_notes.note: Too cooperative. Change 'decided to cooperate' to something that highlights their lack of bond. Suggestion: 'They decided to work together, as it is the most efficient way to ensure no one person takes all the blame.'

Marisol is too helpful. Make her 'vision' more about her own obsession. Suggestion: Change 'Winston, you may help' to 'Winston, I have found a task suited to your particular temperament: alphabetizing these footnotes.'
Marisol's consideration of Winston is too genuine. Suggestion: 'The guild's office is in a quiet basement, which will prevent Winston from making those distressing little noises.'

Chester's internal monologue is a bit generic. Lean into the pixel-art nature of his brain. Suggestion: 'Chester nodded politely. He was currently wondering if he could fit a whole slice of pizza into his inventory slot.'

The 'human wedge' joke is good, but make it more a backhanded compliment. Suggestion: 'Winston, your unique proportions make you the perfect tool for this task!' Marisol beamed, ignoring how Winston looked like he was contemplating a sudden exit from the physical plane.

Winston's reaction to the alarm is too positive ('refreshing change'). He should be terrified but polite. Suggestion: 'Mercy!' cried Winston. He found the alarm to be a very loud way of reminding him that he was still alive.

The 'compatible group' line is close, but needs more 1950s narrator irony. Suggestion: 'They were a most compatible group, in the way that three different types of mismatched luggage are all compatible with the same overhead bin.'
Chester's 'resizing' is a great visual gag. Add a subtle map pun here. Suggestion: 'Chester tried to resize the smudge, but he found himself completely off-axis.'

The ending is the strongest part of the draft, but could be punchier. Suggestion: 'They walked away together, each cherishing the wonderful silence that comes when one has finally run out of things to say to another person.'
